extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and practitioners of art and architecture (readers of Ruskin; art-historians and architects interested in Gothic style)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and judge features of Gothic architecture according to Ruskin's criteria (e.g., naturalism, veracity, rigidity, redundancy, vegetation, grotesque). Useful for stylistic analysis, critique, or historically-informed design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three classes of artists: Purist, Naturalist, Sensualist
rubrics_metrics.description: The three classes may be likened to men reaping wheat: the Purists take the fine flour, the Sensualists the chaff and straw, and the Naturalists take all home and make their cake of the one and their couch of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines baseline evaluative categories for artworks: Purists select and idealize elements 'good for him'; Sensualists 'fill themselves with the husks that the swine did eat' (delight in foul or purely exciting detail); Naturalists represent the whole of nature (both grain and chaff). Use these categories to classify an artist's temperament and to judge whether treatment of subject is selective, indulgent, or comprehensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalism (as essential Gothic characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Gothic builders were 'Naturalists' — men who unite fact with design, adding to design a love of fact and truthfulness in representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess Gothic work for its truthful rendering of real forms (leaves, human countenance, common incidents). Naturalism implies sympathy with the full range of life — haste, anger, sensuality, pride, fortitude, faith — and making a 'majestic harmony' out of all. Naturalism is considered central and noble in Gothic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness / Veracity
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic work is characterised by 'truthfulness' — a love of veracity which influences design, making decorative and sculptural elements more like real leaves, flames, etc., rather than conventionalized motifs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge ornament and symbolism by how faithfully they render the observed truth of forms and actions. Note caveat: love of truth can be misdirected (seizing on surface truth instead of inner meaning) or rashly boastful; true veracity requires thought and discrimination, not mere display of fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness in imaginative representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Gothic mind realizes imaginative truths as fully as actual ones — e.g., instead of leaving symbolic signs that need interpretation, the Gothic inventor 'makes the fire as like real fire as he can.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether symbolic or supernatural subjects are rendered in ways that convey their inner meaning, not merely imitated superficially. Beware of substituting literalism for appropriate symbolic expression: sometimes a more abstract or conventional sign better communicates an inner truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veracity in portraiture and everyday detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic sculpture records 'the most familiar scenes and most simple subjects,' filling backgrounds with 'vivid and curious representations of the commonest incidents of daily life' and producing 'copious records' of domestic customs and inferior arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value inclusion of ordinary life and honest portraiture: not elevating kings into demi-gods nor saints into archangels, but giving full measure of kingliness/sanctity mixed with recorded faults. Assess breadth and equity of delineation — does the work include social detail that informs historical understanding?

rubrics_metrics.name: Fondness for vegetation (vegetative forms as a primary subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic workmen had a 'peculiar fondness for the forms of Vegetation' and struggled to render leaves, tendrils, and flowers with as much accuracy as compatible with design and material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing Gothic ornament, note careful study and accurate rendering of foliage and plant-forms. This tendency signals refinement, rural/peaceful life, and a temper suited to natural science and domestic wisdom. Excessively conventional or meagre foliage counts against the Gothic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility and frankness (Christian humility expressed in work)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Gothic mind's humility confesses the imperfection of the workman and subject; Gothic work shows 'frankness' in confessing faults and mixing sanctity with due record of human error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humility in architecture as readiness to include imperfect or ordinary features rather than hiding them; humility also supports inclusiveness (decoration that appeals to both rude and refined minds). Consider whether a work's ornament and representation are unpretentious and socially communicative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque (delight in the fantastic and ludicrous)
rubrics_metrics.description: A universal instinct of the Gothic imagination is the tendency to delight in fantastic and ludicrous images — the 'GROTESQUE' is listed as an essential element of the Gothic mind (definition deferred).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for an appetite for the bizarre, comic, and fantastical in Gothic ornament and sculpture. Though Ruskin defers full definition, inclusion of grotesque elements is a characteristic sign; judge whether such elements enrich or degenerate the design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity (active rigidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigidity: 'not merely stable, but active rigidity; the peculiar energy which gives tension to movement, and stiffness to resistance... an elastic tension and communication of force from part to part.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess lines, vaults, tracery and ornament for 'active' stiffness — sharp energy, angularity, prickly independence (crockets, pinnacles). Consider causes (rapid working, climate, material) and effects: rigidity imparts vigor but in excess can cause 'frivolity of division' or perversity of purpose. Good Gothic balances rigidity with other elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudeness and love of change (changefulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudeness (confession of imperfection) and the love of change are primary Gothic impulses: rudeness springs from humility and unrefined material; changefulness from a restless creative energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the acceptability of roughness and varied ornament as expressions of humility and collective labor. Excessive rudeness or feverish change can be morbid; the best Gothic unites rudeness and change with thoughtful design so they do not become mere coarseness or caprice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundance (accumulation of ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: Redundance: the 'uncalculating bestowal of the wealth of its labor' — a profuse accumulation of ornament characteristic of many Gothic façades; part of the school's humility and its appeal to both rude and refined minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the balance between richness and simplicity: redundancy can be noble (unselfish sacrifice, sympathy with material universe) and necessary to appeal across social ranks, but excessive ornament may mask feebleness. A good Gothic façade may use redundance to achieve grandeur without losing repose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of fact with design (men of both design and fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic builders 'belong to the central or greatest rank' because they unite 'fact with design'; their special part is 'truthfulness' rather than greater inventiveness of arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating Gothic architecture, check how well factual observation (honest detail, local materials, natural forms) is integrated into disciplined design. The ideal Gothic neither abandons design to fact nor falsifies fact for design — it harmonises both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of shortsightedness and misdirected love of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Both Naturalists and Purists may err from 'shortness of sight' — seeing only outsides or trivial points; the love of truth may be misdirected by thoughtlessness or vanity, seizing on surface truth instead of inner truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use critical discrimination: value deep, penetrating observation (color against the sky, inner significance) over mere anatomical or superficial detail. Penalize 'vulgar Naturalists' who show only surface facts, and 'vulgar Purists' whose choices reveal narrowness or silliness.
